litigation_timing.support: Amendment No. 12 (passed 1991-02-12) is the 'dirty trick' legislation: s. 1 adds s. 6A to Basic Law: The Knesset (an MK who left his faction without resigning may not stand at the next election on a list of a faction of the outgoing Knesset; 'leaving' includes voting against the faction in a confidence vote for consideration; 'consideration' includes a promised list place or appointment); s. 2 amends the Knesset Elections Law (faction splits, House Committee determination with appeal to the Jerusalem District Court, s. 57A ban on list-place agreements before the 90th day before elections); s. 3 amends Basic Law: The Government: s. 5(b1) (defector may not be a minister in that Knesset), s. 13A (agreements on ministerial or deputy-ministerial office only by authorized faction representatives; no agreement not to remove a person from office; no guarantee in money, money's worth, service or any benefit to secure such an agreement, any such guarantee void), s. 13B (coalition agreements to be deposited with the Knesset Secretary within three days and before the government presents itself), s. 34(b) (defector may not be deputy minister). HCJ 1635/90 Zerzevsky v. Prime Minister, PD 45(1) 749, a petition by a Likud Central Committee member to set aside the Likud's 11 April 1990 agreement with Modai's 'Party for the Advancement of the Zionist Idea' (list places, ministerial posts, financial guarantees), was decided 25 February 1991, thirteen days after passage, so it was pending before the Supreme Court when the amendment passed, and it concerned the rule the amendment changed (the validity of political agreements on office backed by guarantees, the subject of the new s. 13A(c)). The amendment also followed a judgment already given: HCJ 1601/90 Shalit v. Peres, PD 44(3) 353, judgment 8 May 1990, which ordered publication of coalition agreements and which the new s. 13B codifies.
litigation_timing.note: Pending: HCJ 1635/90 Zerzevsky v. Prime Minister, judgment 1991-02-25 (date from a single secondary source; see deviations). Judgment already given and responded to by s. 13B: HCJ 1601/90 Shalit v. Peres, 1990-05-08. If Zerzevsky was in fact decided before 1991-02-12 the value becomes No.

litigation_timing.source: Second pass, whole law. Enactment: Nevo consolidated text of חוק-יסוד: הממשלה, תשנ"ב-1992 (www.nevo.co.il/law_html/law19/btl0631.htm), read 2026-10-22 from the Wayback Machine capture of 2021-11-21 (section list; s. 17 פרסום הסכמים; s. 18 סייג להסכם, including s. 18(b) voiding any guarantee given to secure an agreement on office; s. 19 הבעת אי-אמון; ss. 20-22 dissolution; ss. 23-29 resignation, removal and acting PM; s. 58 amending Basic Law: The State Economy). Hebrew Wikipedia article 'חוק יסוד: הממשלה (1992)' (raw wikitext via API, read 2026-10-22), sections 'רקע' and the legislative-process paragraphs (preliminary reading of the four private bills 1990-03-19, first reading 1990-05-28, second/third readings begun 1992-01-02 to 01-07, bill returned to committee 1992-01-13, passed 1992-03-18). Litigation searches, all 2026-10-22: Hebrew Wikipedia API searches for 'בג"ץ /91 ראש הממשלה עתירה 1991', 'בג"ץ /92 ראש הממשלה 1992 עתירה שמיר', '"1523/90"', '"פ"ד מו" בג"ץ הממשלה 1992', '"פ"ד מה" בג"ץ ראש הממשלה 1991', 'בג"ץ שמיר עתירה 1992 ממשלת מעבר', '"לוי נ' ראש הממשלה" 1990'; Hebrew Wikipedia articles read for lines citing בג"ץ or עתירה: 'הכנסת השתים עשרה', 'ממשלת ישראל העשרים וארבע', 'הצעת אי-אמון', 'ממשלת מעבר', 'חוק יסוד: הכנסת', 'הסכם קואליציוני', 'בג"ץ שליט נגד פרס', 'היועץ המשפטי לממשלה'; five WebSearch queries on 1992 petitions concerning the transitional government, dissolution, coalition agreements, appointments and the bill's legislative process (terms recorded in the reader's report).
litigation_timing.support: The law as passed on 1992-03-18 introduced direct election of the Prime Minister concurrent with Knesset elections, special elections, the 45-day presentation of a government requiring Knesset confidence, ministers' qualifications, publication of coalition agreements (s. 17) and restrictions on agreements about office with guarantees declared void (s. 18), no-confidence in the PM by 61 members entailing the Knesset's dissolution (s. 19), dissolution for failure to pass the budget (s. 20), the PM's power to dissolve the Knesset with the President's consent (s. 22), removal of the PM, an acting PM, and, by s. 58, the continuing-budget rule in Basic Law: The State Economy s. 3B. None of the sources or searches disclosed any petition or appeal pending before the Supreme Court on 1992-03-18 concerning government formation, coalition agreements, no-confidence, dissolution, the transitional government's powers or the Prime Minister's powers; the only Supreme Court matters on these subjects located for 1990-92 are HCJ 1601/90 Shalit v. Peres (judgment 1990-05-08) and HCJ 1635/90 Zerzevsky v. Prime Minister (judgment 1991-02-25), both already decided. The first-pass finding for s. 58 (no pending petition on the continuing budget) stands.
litigation_timing.note: Judgments already given that the law responded to, through ss. 17-18 carried forward from Basic Law: The Knesset (Amendment No. 12) of 1991-02-12: HCJ 1601/90 Shalit v. Peres, PD 44(3) 353, judgment 1990-05-08 (publication of coalition agreements, codified in s. 17); HCJ 1635/90 Zerzevsky v. Prime Minister, PD 45(1) 749, judgment 1991-02-25 (validity of a political agreement backed by a financial guarantee, addressed by s. 18(b)). The principal reform, direct election of the Prime Minister, answered the 1990 political crisis rather than any judgment. HCJ 1523/90 Levi v. Prime Minister was not found in any source and is presumed decided in 1990-91; if it was still pending on 1992-03-18 the row should be recoded Yes.

first_pass_section_58_only.support: Section 58 of Basic Law: The Government (1992), passed 1992-03-18, inserted s. 3B into Basic Law: The State Economy: if the budget law is not passed before the fiscal year begins, the government may spend each month one-twelfth of the previous year's budget (the continuing budget) and incur commitments within set limits. No petition on the continuing budget, on a budget not passed in time, or on the spending authority in such a year was found pending in March 1992. The principal subject of the 1992 law (direct election of the Prime Minister) is covered by another reader and was not coded here.
